35.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of the Word of God in our lives. As believers, we must rely on the Scriptures that are unshakeable and eternal. This encourages us to live according to the truth revealed by God, knowing that nothing can annihilate his authority and promises.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to sanctify' or 'to set apart for sacred use'. In the context of John 10:36, it highlights the divine action by which the Father chose and consecrated Jesus for his saving mission. This sheds light on the divine authority over the Son and the importance of his mission as the Messiah, which is fundamental to understanding the nature of his ministry and his role in the plan of salvation.

This term means 'to send' and is often used to designate a divine mission. In this verse, it emphasizes that Jesus did not come of his own accord, but was sent by the Father, reinforcing the idea of the Son's obedience and submission to the Father's will. This has profound implications for understanding authority and divine mission in the New Testament.

This verb means 'to blaspheme' and implies a word or action that dishonors God. In the context of this verse, it highlights the reaction of the Jews to Jesus' declaration as the Son of God, revealing their misunderstanding and rejection of his divine identity. This reminds us of the importance of recognizing the divinity of Christ and the consequences of his rejection.

This expression means 'Son of God' and is central to Christology. It indicates not only the unique relationship between Jesus and the Father but also his authority and divinity. Recognizing Jesus as the Son of God is fundamental to the Christian faith, as it implies acceptance of his redemptive role and his authority over our lives.

36.epoque: The historical context of this verse is set in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Palestine, a time marked by religious tensions between Jewish authorities and Jesus' teachings.
36.passage: This verse is part of a discourse where Jesus defends his identity and mission against the opposition of religious leaders who accuse him of blasphemy for claiming his divine sonship. This takes place in chapter 10, where he presents himself as the good shepherd.
36.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the notion of blasphemy was taken very seriously, and any claim to divinity was considered a grave offense. The rejection of Jesus by the authorities shows the struggle between divine revelation and human traditions.
36.interpretation: Jesus' affirmation as the Son of God underscores his divine nature and authority. This rejection by religious leaders illustrates the difficulty of recognizing divine truth when it challenges established beliefs.
36.commentaire: John 10:36 reminds us that Jesus, as the Son of God, was sent by the Father to accomplish a sacred mission. This passage invites us to reflect on our own understanding of who Jesus is and to recognize his authority in our lives. As believers, we are called to honor this truth and to live accordingly, witnessing the reality of his divinity in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This term means 'works' and refers to actions, tasks, or accomplishments. In the context of John 10:37, it emphasizes that the works of Jesus are not merely miracles, but manifestations of God's will and nature. This implies a dimension of divine testimony, where Jesus' acts confirm his messianic identity and his relationship with the Father.

The word 'Father' evokes an intimate and personal relationship between God and Jesus, as well as between God and believers. In Jewish culture, the Father is often associated with protection, authority, and the source of all life. The mention of the Father here reinforces the idea that the works of Jesus are in perfect harmony with divine will, thus highlighting his role as the Son of God.

37.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman occupation, and religious tensions were high between the Jews and the Roman authorities, as well as among different Jewish factions. Jesus, as the central figure of emerging Christianity, positions himself in the face of these issues by affirming his divine authority.
37.passage: John 10 addresses the theme of the good shepherd and the relationship between Jesus and his disciples. In this chapter, Jesus defends his ministry and identity as the Son of God, using metaphors to illustrate his mission and his connection with the Father.
37.culture: In Jewish culture, works were often seen as signs of the authenticity of a prophet or a messiah. Miracles and teachings were means by which religious leaders validated their authority and message.
37.interpretation: This verse highlights the importance of Jesus' actions as proof of his divinity. It invites listeners to evaluate his mission not only by his words but also by his works, which testify to his unique relationship with the Father.
37.commentaire: John 10:37 reminds us that our faith must be founded on tangible evidence of God's work in our lives. As believers, we are called to live works that reflect our relationship with Christ, thus showing the world the reality of our faith. This encourages us to examine our own actions and ensure that they glorify God and testify to our commitment to Him.

mots.sens: This term means 'works' and refers to concrete actions, often associated with miracles or acts of divine power. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of Jesus' actions as a testimony to his divine identity. The works are not only proofs of his authority, but they also reveal the unity between the Father and the Son, thereby strengthening the faith of believers.

This verb means 'to believe' and implies a deep and personal trust. It is not merely intellectual assent, but a living faith that engages the whole being. In this verse, Jesus calls his listeners to move beyond their doubts and place their trust in him, not only based on his words but also on his works.

This verb means 'to know' or 'to recognize' and implies a knowledge that goes beyond mere information. It is an intimate and personal understanding that leads to a relationship. In the context of this verse, Jesus invites his interlocutors to recognize the truth of his union with the Father through his works, which is essential for authentic faith.

38.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context where Jesus is teaching in Israel, confronted by the unbelief of the Jewish religious authorities and the crowds. The tensions between Jesus and the religious leaders are palpable as he seeks to reveal his true identity as the Son of God.
38.passage: In John 10, Jesus speaks of himself as the Good Shepherd, contrasting with the false shepherds. Verse 38 emphasizes the importance of Jesus' works as proof of his union with the Father, inviting his listeners to recognize this truth even if they hesitate to believe his words.
38.culture: At that time, miracles were often seen as signs of divine authority. The Jews were expecting a Messiah who would perform powerful works, and Jesus uses this expectation to invite them to see in him the fulfillment of these promises.
38.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that faith should not be based solely on words, but also on actions. Jesus calls his listeners to an active recognition of his divinity through his works, urging them to have a faith that relies on tangible evidence of his ministry.
38.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our faith must be nourished by the works of God in our lives. Jesus invites us to observe and recognize the signs of his presence and action, even when our understanding is limited. As believers, we are called to testify to these works, in order to encourage those who doubt to believe in him.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to seize' or 'to catch.' In the context of John 10:39, it evokes the idea of forcefully seizing someone or attempting to control them. This term underscores the resistance of Jesus' opponents to His divine mission, but also the power of Jesus that escapes their attempts. Spiritually, this reminds us that God's plans cannot be hindered by human intentions.

This verb means 'to escape' or 'to flee out of.' It indicates an action of quickly getting out of a perilous situation. In this verse, it highlights the sovereignty of Jesus who, despite threats, is able to free himself from the hands of those who seek to capture him. Theologically, this reinforces the idea that Jesus is the Good Shepherd who protects His sheep and cannot be stopped by opposing forces.

39.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Palestine, a time marked by religious and political tensions between the Jewish authorities and the Roman occupiers.
39.passage: In John 10, Jesus presents himself as the Good Shepherd, contrasting with the false shepherds. This verse illustrates the hostile reaction of the authorities to His teachings and miracles, and their inability to seize Him, thus revealing His divine nature.
39.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, figures of authority, such as the Pharisees, were often in conflict with those who challenged their teachings. Jesus, as the Messiah, provoked extreme reactions from these religious leaders.
39.interpretation: This verse shows that despite human attempts to control or eliminate Jesus, His divine mission cannot be hindered. It reminds us that God has ultimate control over all situations and that His will will always be accomplished.
39.commentaire: John 10:39 teaches us that, even in the face of opposition, Jesus remains secure in the will of His Father. This encourages us to trust in divine protection in our own struggles. We must remember that, like Jesus, we can rely on God's power to deliver us from difficult situations and to pursue our mission with faith.

mots.sens: This word refers to Jesus, the Savior and the Messiah. It is derived from the Hebrew 'Yeshoua', which means 'Yahweh saves'. In this context, it emphasizes the divine identity of Jesus and His central role in the plan of salvation. The mention of His name here reminds readers of Jesus' authority and mission as the Son of God.

The Jordan is a river that holds great symbolic importance in the Bible, representing the boundary between the Old and New Testaments. It is the place where John the Baptist baptized, marking the beginning of Jesus' ministry. The Jordan also evokes themes of purification and passage to a new life, thus highlighting Jesus' redemptive ministry.

This verb means 'to baptize' and is related to the idea of purification and spiritual initiation. In the context of John the Baptist, baptism symbolized repentance and preparation for the coming of the Messiah. Here, it echoes the work of Jesus who, through His sacrifice, offers definitive purification to believers.

This verb means 'to remain' or 'to stay', and it is often used in the New Testament to express the idea of communion and intimate relationship. In this verse, it underscores the importance of Jesus' presence in a significant place, where He continues His ministry. This reminds believers of the importance of remaining in Christ to receive His life and guidance.

40.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus, a period marked by intense messianic expectation among the Jewish people and tensions with the religious authorities of the time.
40.passage: In this chapter, Jesus faces controversies with the Pharisees regarding His identity and authority. His departure to the Jordan is significant, as He returns to a place of baptism, recalling His connection with John the Baptist and His call to repentance.
40.culture: Baptism was a Jewish practice of purification, but the ministry of John the Baptist introduced a new spiritual dimension, preparing the people to welcome the Messiah. The Jordan, as a place of baptism, is rich in symbolism and history for the Jews.
40.interpretation: The fact that Jesus returns to the Jordan, a place of baptism, emphasizes His role as the one who purifies and transforms. It also evokes the idea that, even in the face of opposition, Jesus remains faithful to His mission of redemption and call to repentance.
40.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of returning to the foundations of our faith, symbolized by baptism. Jesus, by remaining in a place of purification, invites us to reflect on our own relationship with Him and to renew our commitment to His mission. As believers, we are called to remain in Him, to seek His guidance, and to live a life of repentance and transformation.

mots.sens: The name 'Ioannēs' refers to John the Baptist, an important prophet in the New Testament. His role was to prepare the way for Jesus, preaching repentance and announcing the coming of the Messiah. Although he did not perform miracles, his preaching and testimony about Jesus are considered foundational for the Christian faith, highlighting the importance of truth in John's ministry.

The term 'ἀλήθεια' means truth. In the biblical context, truth is often associated with divine revelation and God's faithfulness. Here, the truth proclaimed by John about Jesus underscores the authenticity of the testimony and the necessity of recognizing Jesus as the Son of God, which has profound implications for the faith and lives of believers.

The word 'θαῦμα' translates to miracle or wonder. Although John did not perform miracles, the contrast here highlights the nature of his ministry, which was more focused on the proclamation of truth than on supernatural manifestations. This reminds us that the power of truth can be more impactful than visible signs, inviting believers to base their faith on the word of God.

41.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, a time marked by Roman occupation and intense messianic expectation among the Jewish people. Religious figures like John the Baptist played a crucial role in the spiritual preparation of the people.
41.passage: In this chapter, Jesus presents Himself as the Good Shepherd, and this verse highlights the recognition of His authority by those who hear John's testimony. It emphasizes the importance of truth in spiritual discernment.
41.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, miracles were often seen as signs of a prophet's authenticity. However, here, the emphasis is on John's verbal testimony rather than miraculous acts, highlighting a different dimension of faith.
41.interpretation: This verse teaches us that the truth proclaimed by John the Baptist is a solid foundation for faith in Jesus. The recognition of Jesus as the Messiah rests on revealed truth, not on spectacular manifestations, calling us to a faith anchored in the word of God.
41.commentaire: This passage reminds us that the strength of our testimony lies in the truth we share. Even without miracles, our proclamation of Jesus can have a powerful impact. Let us be faithful witnesses to the truth of Christ, relying on His word to guide our faith and daily lives.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. It is derived from the root 'pistis', which denotes faith or trust. In the context of John 10:42, it emphasizes the act of believing in Jesus as the Messiah, which implies a personal relationship and acceptance of His divinity. The theological significance of this word is immense, as it reveals that faith in Christ is essential for salvation and communion with God.

This term means 'many' or 'numerous'. It evokes a large quantity or plurality, indicating that faith in Jesus was not limited to a few individuals, but touched a wide audience. This underscores the impact of Christ's work and the positive response it elicits from those who hear His message.

This word means 'there' or 'in that place'. It specifies the geographical context where events are taking place, highlighting the importance of the location in the revelation of Jesus. Spiritually, this can be interpreted as a call to recognize that faith can arise in unexpected places, where the truth of Christ is proclaimed.

42.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in a context where Jesus preached in Israel, a period marked by religious and political tensions between the Jews and the Roman occupiers.
42.passage: John 10 describes Jesus as the good shepherd, who knows His sheep and gives them eternal life. Verse 42 highlights the positive response of many listeners to His teaching and miracles.
42.culture: At that time, Jewish faith was deeply rooted in the law and traditions. However, the proclamation of Jesus as the Messiah provoked debates and divisions, but also significant conversions among those open to the truth.
42.interpretation: This verse highlights the power of the revelation of Jesus and the response of sensitive hearts to His call. The faith that arises in this context testifies to the work of the Holy Spirit, who draws people to Christ.
42.commentaire: John 10:42 reminds us that faith in Jesus can manifest in surprising ways and in varied contexts. As believers, we are called to share the Gospel boldly, knowing that God works in the hearts of people, even where we least expect it. This verse encourages us to persevere in our testimony, for the promise of eternal life is offered to all who believe.
